title: Vault & Consul
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by HashiCorp. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: The un-deleted secret
scenarios.situation: You delete a database password at secret/app/db via 'vault kv delete', then realize the app still needs the old value during rollback. With kv-v1 you'd be out of luck — but this mount is kv-v2.
scenarios.prompt: What does kv-v2 give you that kv-v1 doesn't, and how do you recover?
choices: Versioned secrets — 'vault kv undelete' restores the soft-deleted version; 'destroy' is the only irreversible removal
Automatic backup to the storage backend — just restart Vault
kv-v2 delete is a no-op — the secret was never actually deleted
Nothing — kv-v1 and kv-v2 delete identically
scenarios.why: kv-v2 versions every write: delete only soft-deletes (hides) the latest version, undelete restores it, and destroy permanently erases specific versions. kv-v1 has no versions — delete is final. This is why kv-v2 is the default choice for human-managed secrets, with check-and-set (CAS) for safe concurrent writes.
scenarios.hint: Which kv version keeps history of every write?

scenarios.title: Where did my secret go?
scenarios.situation: You run 'vault kv put secret/app/db password=hunter2' and then 'vault kv get secret/app/db' — but a policy allowing read on 'secret/app/db' is denied.
scenarios.prompt: What path subtlety of kv-v2 explains the denial?
choices: kv-v2's API inserts data/ and metadata/ under the mount — the policy must allow 'secret/data/app/db', not 'secret/app/db'
The secret wasn't written — kv put needs the -v2 flag
Policies apply to mounts, not paths — allow 'secret/' instead
kv get reads from a different mount than kv put writes to
scenarios.why: The CLI hides it, but kv-v2's HTTP API is mount + data/ + path for reads/writes and mount + metadata/ + path for version management. Policies match the real API paths, so kv-v2 policies must use secret/data/... (and secret/metadata/... for version ops). This is the single most common Vault policy bug.
scenarios.hint: What does the CLI abstract away that policies must match exactly?

scenarios.title: The shared database password
scenarios.situation: Fifteen microservices share one Postgres password stored in Vault. When it's rotated, all fifteen must be updated simultaneously — last rotation caused a 20-minute outage.
scenarios.prompt: Which secrets engine eliminates the shared static credential?
choices: The database secrets engine — each service gets unique, short-lived dynamic credentials that Vault creates and revokes automatically
The transit engine — it encrypts the shared password more strongly
The SSH engine — it replaces database passwords with SSH keys
A second kv mount — splitting the password across mounts improves rotation
scenarios.why: The database engine generates per-client dynamic credentials (CREATE ROLE with TTL), so there's no shared password to rotate in lockstep — each lease simply expires and the service fetches a fresh one. Static roles can still rotate a stored password on a schedule, but dynamic creds remove the coordination problem entirely.
scenarios.hint: What if every service had its own password that expired automatically?

scenarios.title: Certificates without the ticket queue
scenarios.situation: Developers wait 3 days for ops to issue TLS certificates from the corporate CA. You want short-lived certs issued on demand via API with automatic expiry.
scenarios.prompt: Which engine fits, and what do roles control?
choices: The PKI engine — roles define allowed domains, TTLs, key types, and whether clients or servers certs are issued
The kv engine — store pre-generated certs and rotate them manually
The transit engine — it signs CSRs with HMAC
The identity engine — it issues X.509 directly to entities
scenarios.why: Vault's PKI engine acts as an internal CA: mount it, configure roles constraining what can be issued (allowed_domains, max_ttl, key_bits), and clients request certs via API. Short TTLs (hours/days) shrink the revocation problem — expired certs simply stop working. Transit does encryption-as-a-service, not certificates.
scenarios.hint: Which engine's whole job is acting as a certificate authority?

scenarios.title: Encrypt without touching keys
scenarios.situation: The app must encrypt PII before writing to the database, but the security team forbids the app from ever seeing encryption keys. Key rotation must not require re-encrypting all data at once.
scenarios.prompt: How does the transit engine solve this?
choices: The app sends plaintext to transit/encrypt/<key> and stores the ciphertext — Vault holds the keys; rotation creates a new key version while old versions still decrypt
Transit gives the app the key over mTLS once at startup
Store the key in kv and have the app encrypt locally — same thing
Transit encrypts the database volume itself
scenarios.why: Transit is encryption-as-a-service: the app never handles key material, only ciphertext. Key rotation is versioned — new data encrypts with the latest version while previous versions remain available for decryption, so there's no big-bang re-encryption. Convergent encryption and datakey modes cover advanced needs.
scenarios.hint: What if the app only ever saw ciphertext and never the key?

scenarios.title: Two teams, one secret mount
scenarios.situation: Team A and Team B both need kv secrets, but Team A must never read Team B's. They're currently sharing the single default 'secret/' mount with one broad policy.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two clean ways to isolate them?
choices: Separate mounts (secret-team-a/, secret-team-b/) with per-mount policies, or path-scoped policies under one mount (secret/data/team-a/* vs team-b/*)
Run two Vault clusters — mounts can't provide isolation
Give both teams the root token and trust them
Rename the mount daily so nobody finds the other team's secrets
scenarios.why: Vault's isolation primitives are mounts and policy paths. Separate mounts give the strongest boundary (also separable audit and tune settings); path-scoped policies under one mount work fine for cooperative teams. Either way, least-privilege policies replace the broad shared one — never hand out root tokens.
scenarios.hint: What are Vault's two levels of namespacing for secrets?

scenarios.title: CI needs Vault access
scenarios.situation: Your CI pipeline needs database credentials from Vault. Hardcoding a token in CI variables is banned — tokens leak and never expire cleanly.
scenarios.prompt: Which auth method fits machines, and what are its two halves?
choices: AppRole — the role_id identifies the machine (like a username) and the secret_id authenticates it (like a password); both are required to get a token
Userpass — create a CI user with a password in the pipeline
Token auth — hardcode a token but rotate it yearly
Disable auth — CI runs in a trusted network
scenarios.why: AppRole is designed for machines: role_id is non-secret identity, secret_id is the secret credential — delivered separately (ideally via different channels). The pair is exchanged for a short-lived token. Bound CIDRs, secret_id TTLs, and per-role policies scope it tightly. userpass is for humans; hardcoded tokens are the anti-pattern.
scenarios.hint: Which method splits machine identity into a public half and a secret half?

scenarios.title: Pods authenticating to Vault
scenarios.situation: App Pods in namespace 'payments' need secrets. You don't want to inject long-lived tokens into Pod specs.
scenarios.prompt: How does the Kubernetes auth method establish trust?
choices: Vault validates the Pod's projected service-account JWT against the K8s API; roles bind specific service accounts/namespaces to policies
Pods send their node name — Vault trusts all kubelets
Mount the Vault root token as a Secret in every Pod
Kubernetes auth doesn't exist — use AppRole with sidecars
scenarios.why: The K8s auth method: Vault is configured with the cluster's API endpoint and CA; the Pod presents its service-account token (JWT); Vault verifies it with the K8s TokenReview API and checks it against role bindings (bound_service_account_names, bound_service_account_namespaces). The Vault Agent injector or app then exchanges it for a Vault token — no static secrets in specs.
scenarios.hint: What identity does every Pod already carry that a third party can verify?

scenarios.title: Service vs batch tokens
scenarios.situation: A high-throughput proxy needs a Vault token per request (10k/sec). Service tokens work but the storage backend is groaning under lease writes.
scenarios.prompt: What token type fits, and what do you give up?
choices: Batch tokens — lightweight, no storage writes, but non-renewable, non-persistent (can't survive restart), and can't create children
Root tokens — fastest because they skip policy checks
Longer TTLs on service tokens — same cost, fewer renewals
One shared service token for all requests — simplest
scenarios.why: Batch tokens are encrypted blobs (not stored server-side): cheap to create at massive scale, ideal for ephemeral high-volume use. Trade-offs: fixed TTL (no renewal), lost on Vault restart, no child tokens, limited capabilities. Service tokens are the persistent, renewable default for interactive/long-lived use.
scenarios.hint: What costs a storage write on every token creation?

scenarios.title: Humans need in too
scenarios.situation: Engineers currently share the root token (everyone knows it). You need per-person login tied to company identities with group-based policies.
scenarios.prompt: What is the migration path?
choices: Enable userpass as a stopgap, then move to LDAP or OIDC/JWT auth mapping IdP groups to Vault policies — revoke the shared root token and generate it only via Shamir ceremony when needed
Keep the shared root token but change it monthly
Create one AppRole per engineer — AppRole is for humans
Disable the root token — it's not needed after init
scenarios.why: Humans should auth via the company IdP: LDAP (bind + group mapping) or OIDC (SSO with group claims mapped to policies via groups/roles). This gives per-person audit trails and instant deprovisioning. The root token should be revoked after initial setup (it can be regenerated via unseal keys if ever truly needed). AppRole is for machines, not people.
scenarios.hint: Where do your engineers' identities already live?

scenarios.title: The token that lived forever
scenarios.situation: An app's Vault token has TTL 768h and is renewed forever. A leaked token from 6 months ago is still valid — the blast radius is unbounded in time.
scenarios.prompt: How do TTLs and max TTLs bound this?
choices: Set short TTLs with max_ttl caps — renewals can't exceed max_ttl, forcing periodic re-authentication and bounding any leak's lifetime
TTLs don't matter — leaked tokens can't be used from other IPs
Set TTL to 0 — that means infinite, which is fine for apps
Delete the token — apps don't need tokens
scenarios.why: Token TTL is the initial lifetime; each renewal extends it but never beyond max_ttl (explicit or mount/system default). Short TTLs (minutes–hours) + re-auth (e.g., Vault Agent auto-auth) mean a leaked token dies quickly. Periodic tokens have a fixed period; orphan tokens survive parent revocation — choose deliberately.
scenarios.hint: What stops a token from being renewed forever?

scenarios.title: First login to a new cluster
scenarios.situation: Vault is initialized and unsealed. You have the initial root token from 'vault operator init'. You need to log in from the CLI and set up real auth methods.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe bootstrap sequence?
choices: vault login with the root token, enable proper auth methods and policies, create admin users — then revoke the root token
Use the root token for daily operations — it's the admin account
Delete the unseal keys now that Vault is unsealed
Skip login — the CLI works without authentication
scenarios.why: The initial root token is a bootstrap credential: log in, configure real auth (OIDC/LDAP), write least-privilege policies, then 'vault token revoke' the root token. Unseal keys must be safeguarded (Shamir split among key holders) — they're your recovery path. Daily root-token use destroys auditability.
scenarios.hint: Is the root token a setup tool or a daily driver?

scenarios.title: Anatomy of a policy
scenarios.situation: The payments app needs to read DB creds at secret/data/payments/db and list the keys under secret/data/payments/. Nothing else.
scenarios.prompt: What does the correct policy look like?
choices: path "secret/data/payments/db" { capabilities = ["read"] } plus path "secret/metadata/payments/*" { capabilities = ["list"] }
path "secret/payments/db" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] } — kv-v2 needs no data/ prefix
path "*" { capabilities = ["read"] } — simpler and safe enough
Policies use allow/deny booleans, not capabilities
scenarios.why: Vault policies are path + capabilities (create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny). kv-v2 splits data vs metadata paths: reads need secret/data/..., listing versions needs secret/metadata/... (list on data/ doesn't enumerate keys). Least privilege means scoping to exactly the paths needed — never path "*" for an app.
scenarios.hint: Which two path prefixes does kv-v2 split reads and key-listing across?

scenarios.title: Deny overrides everything
scenarios.situation: An admin policy grants broad read access, but the break-glass root CA private key at pki/root must be unreadable by everyone except the security team.
scenarios.prompt: How do you carve out the exception?
choices: Add path "pki/root" { capabilities = ["deny"] } — deny always wins over any allow, and it's evaluated first
Remove the broad policy — exceptions aren't possible
Deny is just a suggestion — use firewall rules instead
Put the key in a different Vault cluster
scenarios.why: In Vault policy evaluation, an explicit deny on a path overrides all allows — it's the carve-out mechanism. Order: exact-path deny beats everything, then most-specific-path match wins among allows. This lets you grant broadly and except narrowly, which is far more maintainable than enumerating every allowed path.
scenarios.hint: When allow and deny both match a path, which wins?

scenarios.title: One policy for every engineer
scenarios.situation: Each engineer needs read/write to their own folder secret/data/users/<their-name>/*. Writing 200 nearly-identical policies is unmaintainable.
scenarios.prompt: How do you write one policy for all of them?
choices: Use identity templating: path "secret/data/users/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" { capabilities = ["create","read","update","delete","list"] }
Policies can't be parameterized — generate 200 files with a script
Use the root policy — it covers everyone
Give everyone the same folder — sharing is simpler
scenarios.why: Policy paths support templating with identity metadata: {{identity.entity.name}}, {{identity.entity.metadata.team}}, etc. One policy then scopes each authenticated entity to its own subtree — evaluated per-request against the caller's identity. This is the standard pattern for self-service secret spaces.
scenarios.hint: What does Vault know about the caller that a policy could interpolate?

scenarios.title: The token that couldn't renew itself
scenarios.situation: An app's token can't renew itself or look up its own metadata — every login method's token gets the 'default' policy, but someone replaced it with a custom minimal policy.
scenarios.prompt: What did they break, and what's the rule?
choices: They dropped the default policy — it grants auth/token/lookup-self, renew-self, and cubbyhole access; always include it alongside app policies
Tokens don't need to renew — the app should re-login every hour
The default policy is deprecated — apps must use root
Token self-management requires the sudo capability
scenarios.why: The 'default' policy (attached to every token unless explicitly excluded) allows a token to look itself up, renew itself, and use its cubbyhole. Replacing it with only app-specific policies breaks self-renewal — a classic outage cause. Rule: default + app policies, never app policies alone.
scenarios.hint: Which policy lets a token manage itself?

scenarios.title: Testing before shipping
scenarios.situation: You wrote a new policy for the CI role. You want to verify it allows exactly the intended paths — without deploying CI and watching it fail.
scenarios.prompt: How do you test a policy's effective permissions?
choices: vault token capabilities <token> <path> — shows the effective capabilities for that token on that path
Policies can't be tested — deploy and hope
Read the HCL carefully — that's the test
vault policy read shows effective permissions
scenarios.why: 'vault token capabilities' evaluates the token's attached policies against a path and prints the resulting capability set — the ground truth of 'can this token do X here'. 'vault policy read' just shows the HCL source. Test with a real token carrying the CI role's policies before wiring CI to it.
scenarios.hint: Which command answers 'what CAN this token do at this path'?

scenarios.title: The operation that needs sudo
scenarios.situation: A policy grants read on sys/mounts, but 'vault secrets list' still fails with permission denied. The docs mention some endpoints require the sudo capability.
scenarios.prompt: What is the sudo capability, and when is it needed?
choices: Certain privileged API endpoints (mount management, root-heavy sys paths) require capabilities=["read","sudo"] — it's Vault's extra-privilege flag, unrelated to OS sudo
sudo capability means the policy was written by root
It's the same as the root policy — just use root
sudo is deprecated — the endpoint must be wrong
scenarios.why: Some Vault API endpoints are marked sudo-protected (they're cluster-sensitive: mounts, auth tuning, audit devices). Accessing them needs the sudo capability in addition to the verb capability. It's not OS sudo — it's Vault's own 'this is extra sensitive' marker. Grant it sparingly, to admin roles only.
scenarios.hint: What marks a Vault API endpoint as extra-sensitive beyond normal RBAC?

scenarios.title: The credential that expires
scenarios.situation: Your app reads dynamic DB creds from Vault at startup. After the TTL (1h), queries start failing with authentication errors — the app never re-reads.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct client pattern for leased secrets?
choices: Renew the lease before TTL expiry (vault lease renew) while within max_ttl, and re-read fresh creds when renewal is no longer possible — or let Vault Agent manage it
Set TTL to 10 years — leases are meant to be permanent
Restart the app hourly — that's the lifecycle
Leases auto-renew forever — the app has a bug elsewhere
scenarios.why: Dynamic secrets carry a lease: TTL (initial lifetime) + max_ttl (renewal ceiling). Clients should renew proactively (at ~70% of TTL) and handle re-read when max_ttl hits. Vault Agent automates this (auto-auth, caching, template rendering to files with SIGHUP/restart hooks). Apps that read-once break on every TTL — the #1 dynamic-secrets integration bug.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the database user when the lease expires unrenewed?

scenarios.title: Revoking a compromised lease
scenarios.situation: A service's dynamic DB credentials may be compromised. You need them dead NOW — not when the TTL expires in 45 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: How do you kill them immediately?
choices: vault lease revoke <lease-id> — Vault runs the revocation statements (drops the DB user) immediately
Wait for TTL expiry — revocation isn't possible
Delete the Vault token — that also drops the DB user
Change the database root password — the only way
scenarios.why: 'vault lease revoke' executes the engine's revocation logic immediately (e.g., DROP USER in the DB) and invalidates the lease — no waiting for TTL. 'vault lease revoke -prefix <path>' revokes families of leases. Revoking the token also revokes its leases (token → lease hierarchy), which is the bulk path during incidents.
scenarios.hint: What does the secrets engine know how to do when told a lease is dead?

scenarios.title: Delivering the secret_id safely
scenarios.situation: You must hand an AppRole secret_id to a new VM. Sending it in chat/email exposes it; the VM needs it exactly once at bootstrap.
scenarios.prompt: How does response wrapping solve the delivery problem?
choices: Wrap it: Vault returns a single-use wrapping token (cubbyhole) — the VM unwraps it once to get the secret_id; the wrapper can't be reused and expires quickly
Email it with 'delete after reading' — equivalent security
Wrapping encrypts the secret permanently — the VM keeps the wrapper
Put the secret_id in the VM image — simplest delivery
scenarios.why: Response wrapping stores the real response in a cubbyhole behind a short-lived, single-use token. The orchestrator passes only the wrapper; the target unwraps (vault unwrap) to retrieve the secret. If intercepted, the interceptor gets one shot before the legitimate unwrap fails loudly (already-unwrapped) — and TTLs bound the window. It's the standard secure-introduction pattern.
scenarios.hint: What if the delivery token could only be used once, and expired in minutes?

scenarios.title: Stop hand-rolling renewal
scenarios.situation: Every app team wrote its own Vault client with renewal loops — half are buggy (missed renewals, thundering herds at TTL boundaries).
scenarios.prompt: What is the standardize-on solution?
choices: Vault Agent — a local daemon handling auto-auth, secret caching, lease renewal, and template rendering to files the app just reads
More code review — the hand-rolled clients are fine
Increase all TTLs to 30 days — fewer renewals, fewer bugs
Remove Vault — static secrets in env vars are simpler
scenarios.why: Vault Agent centralizes the hard parts: auto-auth (AppRole/K8s/JWT), caching (reduces Vault load, survives brief outages), automatic renewal, and template stanza rendering secrets to files (with exec/restart hooks on change). Apps read files — no Vault client code at all. The K8s injector is Agent-as-sidecar for Pods.
scenarios.hint: What if apps never talked to Vault directly at all?

scenarios.title: The legacy app that needs a fixed password
scenarios.situation: A legacy appliance requires a static DB password (it can't do dynamic creds), but you still want automatic rotation every 30 days without manual coordination.
scenarios.prompt: Which database-engine feature fits?
choices: Static roles — Vault stores the credential and rotates it on a schedule (rotation_period), apps read the current value
Dynamic roles — they also produce static passwords
kv-v2 with a calendar reminder — equivalent
Static passwords can't be rotated automatically
scenarios.why: Database static roles manage a fixed username whose password Vault rotates automatically per rotation_period (and can rotate immediately on demand). Apps read the current password from the role's credentials endpoint. It bridges legacy static-credential apps into Vault-managed rotation — the pragmatic middle ground before full dynamic creds.
scenarios.hint: Which role type keeps the username fixed but rotates the password for you?

scenarios.title: Token hierarchy surprise
scenarios.situation: You revoke a team's parent token after an incident — and all their apps' child tokens die too, causing a wider outage than the incident.
scenarios.prompt: What token concept explains this, and when do you avoid it?
choices: Token parent-child hierarchy — revoking a parent revokes its children; use orphan tokens (created with -orphan) for long-lived service tokens that must survive parent revocation
All tokens are independent — the outage was coincidental
Orphan tokens can't be revoked — avoid them always
Token hierarchy only applies to root tokens
scenarios.why: Tokens form a tree: children die with parents (revocation cascades) — useful for bounding session lifetimes. Orphan tokens break the link: they survive parent revocation, ideal for long-lived service identities. Trade-off: orphans need explicit lifecycle management (they won't die when the creator's token does). Choose per use case: sessions → hierarchical, service identities → orphan.
scenarios.hint: What happens to children when a parent token is revoked?

scenarios.title: Consul's moving parts
scenarios.situation: You're deploying Consul. The docs mention clients, servers, gossip, and Raft — and you're unsure how many servers you need.
scenarios.prompt: What is the architecture, and why 3 or 5 servers?
choices: Servers form a Raft quorum (3 or 5 for failure tolerance); clients run on every node, gossip via Serf, and forward RPCs to servers
All agents are equal — run 1 server for simplicity
Servers are stateless — run as many as you like
Clients store the data — servers are just caches
scenarios.why: Consul servers maintain the catalog via Raft consensus — quorum needs 2n+1 (3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2). Clients are lightweight agents on every node: they run health checks, gossip membership via Serf (fast failure detection), and forward requests to servers. Even numbers don't improve fault tolerance (4 tolerates 1, same as 3, with worse quorum math).
scenarios.hint: How many failures can a 3-node Raft quorum survive?

scenarios.title: Finding the payments API
scenarios.situation: Service 'payments' has 5 healthy instances. A client needs to discover them without hardcoded IPs — via DNS and via HTTP.
scenarios.prompt: What are Consul's two discovery interfaces?
choices: DNS: payments.service.consul (A records for healthy instances); HTTP API: /v1/health/service/payments?passing (JSON with addresses/ports)
Only DNS exists — the HTTP API is for config only
Hardcode the IPs — discovery is unreliable
Consul has no DNS — use an external DNS server
scenarios.why: Consul serves DNS on port 8600 (service.consul domain: <service>.service.consul, with tag/datacenter variants) and a rich HTTP API (/v1/catalog, /v1/health). Both filter by health status — only passing instances are returned by default. DNS is the zero-code path; the API gives metadata, tags, and Connect info.
scenarios.hint: What does payments.service.consul resolve to?

scenarios.title: The flapping health check
scenarios.situation: A service's HTTP health check fails intermittently under load, causing Consul to flap it in/out of discovery — clients see intermittent failures.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make health checking robust?
choices: Tune interval/timeout/deregister thresholds, check a cheap endpoint (not a deep dependency chain), and consider TTL checks updated by the app itself
Delete the health check — discovery works without it
Check every second — more checks means more accuracy
Health checks must test the database — deep checks are mandatory
scenarios.why: Health checks (script/http/tcp/TTL/docker) should test the service itself cheaply — a deep check coupling to downstream deps causes cascading flaps. Tune interval vs timeout vs failures-before-critical; set deregister_critical_service_after to prune dead nodes. TTL checks let the app report its own health (heartbeat pattern). Flapping usually means the check is too strict or too deep.
scenarios.hint: Should a health check fail because a downstream dependency is slow?

scenarios.title: mTLS without code changes
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires encrypted service-to-service traffic with mutual authentication. Rewriting 40 services to do mTLS is infeasible.
scenarios.prompt: How does Consul Connect deliver this?
choices: Sidecar proxies (Envoy) per service terminate mTLS using SPIFFE identities issued by Consul's CA — the app talks plaintext to localhost, the mesh encrypts
Connect requires rewriting each service's HTTP client
mTLS is impossible without code changes
Use the KV store to distribute certificates manually
scenarios.why: Consul Connect is a service mesh: each service gets an Envoy sidecar; Consul's CA issues SPIFFE-compatible identities (spiffe://trust-domain/ns/default/dc/dc1/svc/payments); sidecars mutually authenticate and encrypt. Intentions (allow/deny by service identity) add L4/L7 authorization. The app is unaware — it dials localhost:proxy_port.
scenarios.hint: What sits next to each service and handles the crypto for it?

scenarios.title: Who may call payments?
scenarios.situation: Only the 'web' service may call 'payments'. Everything else — including a compromised 'analytics' service — must be denied, even though the network is flat.
scenarios.prompt: How do you express this?
choices: An intention: source web → destination payments: allow, with the default-deny intention catching everything else
Firewall rules per host — intentions are advisory
Rename the services — obscurity is the control
Intentions only allow — deny isn't possible
scenarios.why: Intentions are Connect's authorization layer: allow/deny rules between service identities (not IPs — identity survives rescheduling). Set the default intention to deny, then allow web→payments explicitly. They're enforced by the sidecars at L4 (and L7 with protocol config). This is zero-trust service segmentation without network topology changes.
scenarios.hint: Are intentions based on IPs or on service identities?

scenarios.title: KV for config, not secrets
scenarios.situation: The team stores feature flags in Consul KV and database passwords there too. A junior asks if that's fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is KV appropriate for, and what is the warning?
choices: KV is great for feature flags, service config, leader-election locks — but NOT for secrets (no encryption, ACLs only); use Vault for secrets
KV encrypts everything — fine for passwords
KV is only for service discovery — don't store config
Feature flags don't belong in KV — use environment variables
scenarios.why: Consul KV is a simple, watched key-value store — ideal for dynamic config and coordination (with sessions for distributed locks/leader election). But values are stored unencrypted and replicated in Raft logs — it's not a secret manager. The HashiCorp pairing is deliberate: Consul for discovery/config, Vault for secrets (with Vault Agent templating from both).
scenarios.hint: What does KV lack that a secret manager must have?

scenarios.title: Vault is sealed
scenarios.situation: After a restart, Vault reports 'Sealed: true' and all requests fail with 'Vault is sealed'. You have 3 of 5 Shamir key shards.
scenarios.prompt: What does sealing mean, and how do you recover?
choices: Sealed = the master key is not in memory (nothing decryptable); provide 3 shards via 'vault operator unseal' (x3) to reconstruct it — quorum, not all 5, is needed
Sealed means corrupted — restore from backup
One shard is enough — unseal with any single key
Restart again — sealing is transient
scenarios.why: Vault seals when the master key leaves memory (restart, by request) — a security property: encrypted data is useless without it. Shamir's Secret Sharing splits the key: any threshold (3 of 5) reconstructs it. 'vault operator unseal' each shard until threshold. Auto-unseal (cloud KMS) removes the manual ceremony for production. Never store all shards together.
scenarios.hint: How many shards does the threshold require — all, or a quorum?

scenarios.title: Choosing the storage backend
scenarios.situation: You're deploying Vault HA. Options: Raft integrated storage or external Consul. The team wants the fewest moving parts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the current recommendation?
choices: Raft integrated storage — Vault manages its own replicated log; no separate Consul cluster needed for storage
External Consul is required — Vault can't store its own data
Use a SQL database — Raft is deprecated
Storage backends don't affect HA — pick randomly
scenarios.why: Integrated Raft storage is the recommended backend: Vault nodes replicate via Raft directly (3 or 5 nodes for quorum), snapshots via 'vault operator raft snapshot save/restore'. It removed the Consul-as-storage dependency (Consul is still great for service discovery alongside). Fewer components = fewer failure modes.
scenarios.hint: Which backend lets Vault replicate without another system?

scenarios.title: Backing up Vault
scenarios.situation: You need a disaster-recovery backup of all Vault data (secrets, policies, auth config). The storage is Raft.
scenarios.prompt: What is the backup and restore procedure?
choices: 'vault operator raft snapshot save backup.snap' regularly (automated); restore with 'vault operator raft snapshot restore' on a fresh unsealed cluster
Copy the data directory while Vault runs — consistent backup
Backups aren't needed — Raft replicates everything
Export each secret manually — snapshots don't exist
scenarios.why: Raft snapshots are the DR mechanism: scheduled 'snapshot save' (keep them encrypted/offsite — they contain everything), restore onto fresh nodes. Replication protects against node loss, not against logical disasters (bad policy change, deletion) — that's what backups are for. Test restores periodically; an untested backup is a hope.
scenarios.hint: What protects against a bad change replicated to all nodes?

scenarios.title: Upgrading the Vault cluster
scenarios.situation: Three-node Raft cluster on 1.15, target 1.17. You need zero-secret-loss and minimal downtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe upgrade path?
choices: One node at a time: unseal/standby rotation — upgrade standby nodes first, then step down the active and upgrade it; check the upgrade guide for version-specific notes
Upgrade all nodes simultaneously — Raft handles it
Delete and recreate the cluster — fresh is cleanest
Upgrades aren't needed — Vault is stable
scenarios.why: Rolling upgrade: standby nodes first (they rejoin and catch up via Raft), then failover the active (step-down) and upgrade it. Snapshot before starting. Read the version's upgrade guide — some versions have storage or API changes needing extra steps. Never skip more than one minor version without checking the guide.
scenarios.hint: Which node do you upgrade last, and why?

scenarios.title: Who read the production secret?
scenarios.situation: Compliance asks for a log of every secret access last quarter. Nothing was enabled — Vault has no record.
scenarios.prompt: What should have been configured, and what does it log?
choices: An audit device (file/syslog/socket) — logs every request/response (with sensitive values hashed) to an append-only trail; enable at least one before handling real secrets
Audit devices are optional — the operational logs suffice
Enable it now — it backfills history
Audit logs contain plaintext secrets — avoid them
scenarios.why: Audit devices record authenticated requests and responses (sensitive fields HMAC'd, not plaintext) — the compliance trail for 'who accessed what'. At least one must be enabled (Vault errors otherwise in some configs); use multiple for redundancy. They don't backfill — enable before you need them. Ship them to immutable storage (SIEM).
scenarios.hint: What records every Vault API call with the caller's identity?

scenarios.title: Backing up Consul
scenarios.situation: Consul holds service discovery state and KV config you can't afford to lose. Raft replicates it, but you want point-in-time recovery.
scenarios.prompt: How do you back up Consul?
choices: 'consul snapshot save backup.snap' (ACL token with snapshot:write) on a schedule; restore with 'consul snapshot restore' — test restores regularly
Consul backs itself up — no action needed
Copy /var/lib/consul while running — safe
Snapshots only work on the leader — run it there manually each time
scenarios.why: consul snapshot save captures the Raft state atomically (any server works — the request forwards to the leader). Automate with ACL'd tokens and offsite copies. Restore overwrites state — it's DR, not merge. Like Vault: replication ≠ backup; test the restore path before you need it.
scenarios.hint: What captures Consul's Raft state atomically?

lessons.title: Secrets Engines — Core concepts
concepts: KV engine: the database engine generates per-client dynamic credentials (CREATE ROLE with TTL), so there's no shared password to rotate in lockstep — each lease simply expires and the service fetches a fresh one.

kv-v2 versioning: this is why kv-v2 is the default choice for human-managed secrets, with check-and-set (CAS) for safe concurrent writes. Policies match the real API paths, so kv-v2 policies must use secret/data/...
Policy paths: vault's isolation primitives are mounts and policy paths. This is the single most common Vault policy bug.
Dynamic secrets: static roles can still rotate a stored password on a schedule, but dynamic creds remove the coordination problem entirely.

lessons.title: Auth Methods — Core concepts
concepts: AppRole is designed for machines: role_id is non-secret identity, secret_id is the secret credential — delivered separately (ideally via different channels).

Machine auth: the initial root token is a bootstrap credential: log in, configure real auth (OIDC/LDAP), write least-privilege policies, then 'vault token revoke' the root token. Humans should auth via the company IdP: LDAP (bind + group mapping) or OIDC (SSO with group claims mapped to policies via groups/roles).

Kubernetes auth: the K8s auth method: Vault is configured with the cluster's API endpoint and CA; the Pod presents its service-account token (JWT); Vault verifies it with the K8s TokenReview API and checks it against role bindings (bound_service_account_names, bound_service_account_namespaces).
Service tokens are the persistent, renewable default for interactive/long-lived use.

Tokens: bound CIDRs, secret_id TTLs, and per-role policies scope it tightly. userpass is for humans; hardcoded tokens are the anti-pattern. Batch tokens are encrypted blobs (not stored server-side): cheap to create at massive scale, ideal for ephemeral high-volume use.

lessons.title: Policies — Core concepts
concepts: Policy syntax: in Vault policy evaluation, an explicit deny on a path overrides all allows — it's the carve-out mechanism. The 'default' policy (attached to every token unless explicitly excluded) allows a token to look itself up, renew itself, and use its cubbyhole.

Capabilities: vault policies are path + capabilities (create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny). kv-v2 splits data vs metadata paths: reads need secret/data/..., listing versions needs secret/metadata/...
deny: order: exact-path deny beats everything, then most-specific-path match wins among allows.
Policy paths support templating with identity metadata: {{identity.entity.name}}, {{identity.entity.metadata.team}}, etc. 'vault policy read' just shows the HCL source.
Identity-based policies: rule: default + app policies, never app policies alone. Test with a real token carrying the CI role's policies before wiring CI to it.

lessons.title: Dynamic Secrets — Core concepts
concepts: Leases: revoking the token also revokes its leases (token → lease hierarchy), which is the bulk path during incidents.

Renewal: vault Agent centralizes the hard parts: auto-auth (AppRole/K8s/JWT), caching (reduces Vault load, survives brief outages), automatic renewal, and template stanza rendering secrets to files (with exec/restart hooks on change).

Revocation: orphan tokens break the link: they survive parent revocation, ideal for long-lived service identities. 'vault lease revoke' executes the engine's revocation logic immediately (e.g., DROP USER in the DB) and invalidates the lease — no waiting for TTL.
Incident response: response wrapping stores the real response in a cubbyhole behind a short-lived, single-use token.

lessons.title: Consul Service Mesh — Core concepts
concepts: Raft quorum: consul servers maintain the catalog via Raft consensus — quorum needs 2n+1 (3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2). But values are stored unencrypted and replicated in Raft logs — it's not a secret manager.
Service discovery: consul serves DNS on port 8600 (service.consul domain: <service>.service.consul, with tag/datacenter variants) and a rich HTTP API (/v1/catalog, /v1/health).
DNS is the zero-code path; the API gives metadata, tags, and Connect info.

Health checks (script/http/tcp/TTL/docker) should test the service itself cheaply — a deep check coupling to downstream deps causes cascading flaps. Clients are lightweight agents on every node: they run health checks, gossip membership via Serf (fast failure detection), and forward requests to servers.
Flapping usually means the check is too strict or too deep.

lessons.title: Vault & Consul — Core concepts
concepts: Vault is a secrets manager, not a config store: the KV engine holds static secrets, while dynamic engines (database, PKI, AWS) mint short-lived credentials that expire instead of needing rotation.
Every Vault request is authenticated (token, AppRole, JWT/OIDC, Kubernetes auth) and then authorized by policies — capabilities are per-path, so design least-privilege policies before issuing tokens.
Vault seals protect data at rest: Shamir key shares split trust among humans, while auto-unseal via KMS/HSM lets clusters recover from restarts without 3 AM key ceremonies.
Consul provides service discovery with health checks — the catalog and DNS only advertise passing instances, turning failover from a manual task into an automatic one.
Consul Connect adds a service mesh: sidecar proxies enforce mutual TLS for identity, and intentions declare which services are allowed to communicate.
Consul's KV store is for configuration, not secrets — it lacks Vault's encryption, audit, and lease semantics, so never store credentials there.

example.code:
vault kv put secret/app/db password="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"
vault policy write app-read - <<'EOF'
path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }
EOF
example.walkthrough: The first command writes a generated password into the KV engine. The heredoc defines a policy allowing read-only access under secret/data/app/* (note the /data/ infix for KV v2). Tokens minted against this policy can read app secrets and nothing else.

pitfalls: Common trap: using a root token for automation — root bypasses all policies; mint least-privilege tokens via auth methods instead.
Common trap: treating Consul KV as a secrets store — it is plaintext config distribution without Vault's protections.
Common trap: long-lived static credentials in KV that nobody rotates — prefer dynamic secrets with TTLs.
Common trap: confusing gossip encryption with service-mesh mTLS — gossip encryption protects Consul's chatter, not your application traffic.

simulations.brief: Monday morning: applications start failing with 403s from Vault, and the on-call sees 'permission denied' in the audit log. The secrets themselves are intact. Work the diagnostic steps.
simulations.debrief: 403s with intact secrets point at the authorization layer: expired tokens, revoked leases, or policy changes — not missing data. Check token validity before touching secrets or policies.

evidence:
[2026-10-04 09:02:11] client app-svc-3: permission denied on secret/data/payments/api
[2026-10-04 09:02:12] client app-svc-3: permission denied on secret/data/payments/api
steps.explain: A token about to expire (12s TTL) with only the default policy explains permission denied on a path the policy never allowed. Renew or re-issue with the right policy; the secrets are fine.
options: The KV engine is sealed — unseal Vault
The service token is nearly expired and carries only the default policy
The secrets were deleted over the weekend
steps.symptom: Applications get 403 permission denied reading secrets that still exist.

steps.explain: Tokens outlive the intent they were issued with. Re-issuing the token with the payments policy restores access; deleting the policy would break every other client.
options: Re-issue the service token with the payments policy attached
Delete the payments policy and recreate it
steps.symptom: Token renewed, still 403. Friday's change window touched policies.

evidence: After any token re-issue: update the orchestrator secret store so the new token is distributed; never paste tokens into chat.
steps.explain: Token hygiene: distribute through the orchestrator's secret store, scope TTLs tightly, and never let tokens travel through chat or tickets.
options: Push the new token through the orchestrator's secret store and verify the app recovers
Email the token to the team for speed
Commit the token to the repo for visibility
Disable auth and run open until the incident is over

sections.heading: Secrets Engines
items: KV engine — the database engine generates per-client dynamic credentials (CREATE ROLE with TTL), so there's no shared password to rotate in lockstep — each lease simply expires and the service fetches a fresh one.
Policy paths — vault's isolation primitives are mounts and policy paths. This is the single most common Vault policy bug.
Dynamic secrets — static roles can still rotate a stored password on a schedule, but dynamic creds remove the coordination problem entirely.
Common trap — transit encrypts the database volume itself.
Common trap — policies apply to mounts, not paths.
Common trap — rename the mount daily so nobody finds the other team's secrets.
Common trap — splitting the password across mounts improves rotation.

sections.heading: Auth Methods
items: AppRole is designed for machines — role_id is non-secret identity, secret_id is the secret credential — delivered separately (ideally via different channels).

Machine auth — the initial root token is a bootstrap credential: log in, configure real auth (OIDC/LDAP), write least-privilege policies, then 'vault token revoke' the root token. Humans should auth via the company IdP: LDAP (bind + group mapping) or OIDC (SSO with group…

Kubernetes auth — the K8s auth method: Vault is configured with the cluster's API endpoint and CA; the Pod presents its service-account token (JWT); Vault verifies it with the K8s TokenReview API and checks it against role bindings (bound_service_account_names, bound_service…
Service tokens — are the persistent, renewable default for interactive/long-lived use.

Tokens — bound CIDRs, secret_id TTLs, and per-role policies scope it tightly. userpass is for humans; hardcoded tokens are the anti-pattern. Batch tokens are encrypted blobs (not stored server-side): cheap to create at massive scale, ideal for ephemeral high-volume…
Common trap — longer TTLs on service tokens.
Common trap — mount the Vault root token as a Secret in every Pod.
Common trap — keep the shared root token but change it monthly.
Common trap — one shared service token for all requests.

sections.heading: Policies
items: Policy syntax — in Vault policy evaluation, an explicit deny on a path overrides all allows — it's the carve-out mechanism. The 'default' policy (attached to every token unless explicitly excluded) allows a token to look itself up, renew itself, and use its cubbyhole.

Capabilities — vault policies are path + capabilities (create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny). kv-v2 splits data vs metadata paths: reads need secret/data/..., listing versions needs secret/metadata/...
Policy paths support templating with identity metadata — {{identity.entity.name}}, {{identity.entity.metadata.team}}, etc. 'vault policy read' just shows the HCL source.
Identity-based policies — rule: default + app policies, never app policies alone. Test with a real token carrying the CI role's policies before wiring CI to it.
Common trap — token self-management requires the sudo capability.
Common trap — sudo capability means the policy was written by root.
Common trap — policies use allow/deny booleans, not capabilities.
Common trap — vault policy read shows effective permissions.

sections.heading: Dynamic Secrets
items: Leases — revoking the token also revokes its leases (token → lease hierarchy), which is the bulk path during incidents.

Renewal — vault Agent centralizes the hard parts: auto-auth (AppRole/K8s/JWT), caching (reduces Vault load, survives brief outages), automatic renewal, and template stanza rendering secrets to files (with exec/restart hooks on change).

Revocation — orphan tokens break the link: they survive parent revocation, ideal for long-lived service identities. 'vault lease revoke' executes the engine's revocation logic immediately (e.g., DROP USER in the DB) and invalidates the lease — no waiting for TTL.
Incident response — response wrapping stores the real response in a cubbyhole behind a short-lived, single-use token.
Common trap — token hierarchy only applies to root tokens.
Common trap — static secrets in env vars are simpler.
Common trap — wrapping encrypts the secret permanently.
Common trap — static passwords can't be rotated automatically.

sections.heading: Consul Service Mesh
items: Raft quorum — consul servers maintain the catalog via Raft consensus — quorum needs 2n+1 (3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2). But values are stored unencrypted and replicated in Raft logs — it's not a secret manager.
Service discovery — consul serves DNS on port 8600 (service.consul domain: <service>.service.consul, with tag/datacenter variants) and a rich HTTP API (/v1/catalog, /v1/health).
DNS — is the zero-code path; the API gives metadata, tags, and Connect info.

Health — Health checks (script/http/tcp/TTL/docker) should test the service itself cheaply — a deep check coupling to downstream deps causes cascading flaps. Clients are lightweight agents on every node: they run health checks, gossip membership via Serf (fast failu…
Flapping usually — means the check is too strict or too deep.
Common trap — connect requires rewriting each service's HTTP client.
Common trap — health checks must test the database.
Common trap — use the KV store to distribute certificates manually.
Common trap — use an external DNS server.

sections.heading: Operations
items: Shamir's Secret Sharing splits the key — any threshold (3 of 5) reconstructs it.

Raft storage — integrated Raft storage is the recommended backend: Vault nodes replicate via Raft directly (3 or 5 nodes for quorum), snapshots via 'vault operator raft snapshot save/restore'. Rolling upgrade: standby nodes first (they rejoin and catch up via Raft), then…

HA — HA: audit devices record authenticated requests and responses (sensitive fields HMAC'd, not plaintext) — the compliance trail for 'who accessed what'. Raft snapshots are the DR mechanism: scheduled 'snapshot save' (keep them encrypted/offsite — they contain…
Backup — test restores periodically; an untested backup is a hope. Like Vault: replication ≠ backup; test the restore path before you need it.
Raft snapshots — consul snapshot save captures the Raft state atomically (any server works — the request forwards to the leader).
Common trap — audit logs contain plaintext secrets.
Common trap — copy the data directory while Vault runs.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Secrets Engines: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Auth Methods lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Policies terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
